_work.title: Astrological Compendium — Irshad-i Usturlāb and Seven Treatises (Princeton OPenn Islamic MSS, Persian 1670)
_work.blurb: A Persian astrological compendium copied in 1670 CE (AH 1081), comprising seven treatises on astrology, the astrolabe, astronomical tables, and astrological judgment (Princeton University Library, OPenn Islamic Manuscripts, figgy 68f32e92, ark:/88435/dc41687w42j). The primary work is Irshād-i Usṭurlāb (Guidance on the Astrolabe) by Nāṣir ibn Ḥaydar; further treatises cover lunar eclipses, planetary risings and settings, astronomical tables (zīj), Maṭāliʻʹnāmah (Book of Ascendants) by Abū Al-Khayr Muḥammad Taqī Fārsī, and astrological judgments drawn from the tradition of Abū Maʻshar. The manuscript is written in elegant Persian nastaʻlīq script with extensive red-ink rubrication marking chapter headings and key technical terms. The codex is physically extraordinary: bound in fine black leather with elaborate gold-tooled mandorla binding — a large polylobed central medallion (shamseh) surrounded by arabesque filigree tooling on both front and back covers, with cartouches containing calligraphic owner inscriptions on the vertical axis. Two smaller diamond cartouches and a chain-pattern gilt border complete the design. The binding bears the name Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad Bāqir on the pendant cartouches. The manuscript passed through distinguished later ownership: it belonged to Muḥammad ʻAlī al-Iṣfahānī, then to Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan (the Swiss-based diplomat and art collector who assembled one of the finest Islamic manuscript libraries of the 20th century), and was acquired by Lawrence J. Schoenberg in 2001 before reaching Princeton. The front matter includes an ownership leaf (fol. 1r) covered with astrological calculations and multiple owner seals from its provenance chain, and the text contains a formal astrological planetary classification table (fol. 78r) with symbolic planetary headers and six rows of descriptive text for each planet's characteristics.

_work.creator: primary: Nāṣir ibn Ḥaydar (Irshād-i Usṭurlāb); further: Abū Al-Khayr Muḥammad Taqī Fārsī (Maṭāliʻʹnāmah); tradition of Abū Maʻshar

entries.title: Persian Gilt Mandorla Binding — Front Cover with Gold-Tooled Shamseh (1670 CE)
entries.medium: bookbinding, black leather, gold tooling, mandorla design
entries.summary: The front cover of the Princeton Persian astrological compendium (OPenn Islamic MSS, 1670 CE), displaying a masterwork of Safavid-era Persian bookbinding in gold-tooled black leather. The composition follows the standard shamseh format used for fine Persian codices: a large central polylobed oval medallion (the shamseh/shamsa — 'sun') filled with dense arabesque and floral filigree executed in gold tooling against the black leather, with the lobed outline of the medallion itself created by a precisely incised and gilt border. The central medallion is flanked above and below by the vertical axis cartouches: two rectangular panels with calligraphic text in gilt identifying the owner or dedicatee (the catalog records the name Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad Bāqir). Above and below the cartouches, diamond-shaped corner medallions in gold anchor the vertical composition. The entire design is enclosed within a multi-rule gold frame border running around all four edges, with a floral/arabesque chain pattern outside the innermost rule. This type of binding — black leather ground, central shamseh, vertical cartouches, diamond corners, chain-border frame — represents the classic repertoire of Persian court bookbinding from the Safavid period through the 18th century, and was produced for manuscripts intended for wealthy or aristocratic owners. This specific copy belonged to a series of distinguished collectors including Muhammad Ali al-Isfahani, Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan, and Lawrence J. Schoenberg before reaching Princeton.

entries.title: Ownership Leaf with Owner Seals and Astrological Calculations (f. 1r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, circular seals, handwritten calculations
entries.summary: The first text leaf (fol. 1 recto) of the Princeton Persian astrological compendium (OPenn Islamic MSS, 1670 CE), serving as a combined provenance leaf and working calculation page. The upper portion of the page is densely covered with astrological ephemeris calculations: columns of numerals in multiple rows recording planetary positions, degrees, minutes, and year-counts — calculations typical of a working astrologer using the MS for active consultation. Number sequences include values in the hundreds and thousands (٩٦٣١٥٦, ٧٦٠٦٣٤, ٨١٠٨٤, etc.) arranged in groups consistent with astrological table computation. The middle section of the page bears at least two prominent circular seals impressed in ink: one reddish seal with Arabic/Persian calligraphic text in its interior (an ownership or library seal), and one grayish circular seal with text and design elements. Surrounding the seals are handwritten ownership inscriptions in Arabic and Persian recording the manuscript's transmission through successive owners. Additional smaller seal impressions appear in the lower portion. Persian marginal glosses and jottings surround the entire page. This accumulation of seals, calculations, and ownership records on a single page is characteristic of practical working manuscripts that circulated through scholarly households over generations, with each owner contributing their mark to the record of transmission. The specific sequence of owners (Muḥammad ʻAlī al-Iṣfahānī → Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan → Lawrence J. Schoenberg → Princeton) represents one of the finest collector chains for any Islamic manuscript in Princeton's holdings.

entries.title: Astrological Planetary Classification Table — Seven Planets with Symbolic Headers (f. 78r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink and red ink on paper, ruled table with symbolic headers
entries.summary: Folio 78 recto of the Princeton Persian astrological compendium (OPenn Islamic MSS, 1670 CE), containing a formal astrological planetary classification table. The page divides into two zones: the upper half contains dense Persian nastaʻlīq text in the main body with red-ink rubrication for key technical terms, and the lower half presents a ruled table with a red-ink border encompassing the entire grid. The table has approximately 7–8 columns, one for each classical planet (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon), with the header row of each column bearing a small pictographic or abbreviated symbol identifying the planet — the visual markers visible in the header cells include curved and angular forms consistent with Arabic abbreviations of planetary names (زحل = Saturn, مشتري = Jupiter, مريخ = Mars, etc.) or simplified astrological glyphs. Below the header row are 6 rows of Persian text, each row recording a category of astrological classification for each planet — possibly covering the planet's nature (hot/cold/wet/dry), its domicile (sign it rules), its exaltation, its day/night distinction, its relation to the four elements, or other standard attributes from Persian astrological tradition. Below the table, a red-ink section heading reads 'نتیجه اجزاء' (Natijah-yi ajzā' — Conclusions/Results of the Parts), indicating this table concludes a longer discussion of planetary classification. The formal ruled table with symbolic column headers is a standard format for Persian astrological jadāwil (tables) used to systematize planetary data for practical horoscopy and the astrological judgment of charts (aḥkām al-nujūm).

entries.title: Persian Gilt Mandorla Binding — Back Cover with Gold-Tooled Shamseh (1670 CE)
entries.medium: bookbinding, black leather, gold tooling, mandorla design
entries.summary: The back cover of the Princeton Persian astrological compendium (OPenn Islamic MSS, 1670 CE), the mirror composition to the front cover (fol. front, c000). The back cover displays the same black leather gilt-tooled mandorla design: a large central polylobed shamseh medallion filled with arabesque filigree in gold tooling, flanked by two calligraphic cartouches on the vertical axis bearing the owner's name in gilt script, with diamond medallions above and below, all enclosed within a chain-pattern gold border running around the four edges. The back cover retains the same degree of gilt preservation as the front, though slight variations in the gold tone and slight separation at one corner of the leather reveal the aging of the binding over its 350-year history. Together, the front and back covers (c000 and c343) constitute a complete example of a Safavid-tradition Persian bookbinding intended for a manuscript of learning — the geometric precision of the shamseh center, the quality of the arabesque tooling, and the gilt cartouches all signal a production intended for educated aristocratic patronage rather than commercial circulation. The binding passed through the collections of Muḥammad ʻAlī al-Iṣfahānī and Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan before reaching Princeton, representing the high-end end of Persian manuscript collecting history.
